strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underserved gap: existing metrics (FVD, VBench, MEt3R) either ignore geometric distortion or are confounded by valid foreground motion; the paper clearly articulates this via a 'content-over-motion' vs 'fragility-to-motion' framing.

The core idea—partitioning the static background into depth-coherent sub-regions and measuring divergence among independently estimated local camera poses—is physically grounded and intuitively sound, and cleanly disentangles background rigidity from foreground dynamics via explicit motion segmentation.

Extensive empirical validation beyond a single benchmark table: controlled synthetic perturbation experiments (warping, perspective squeeze, depth warp) show monotonic sensitivity to injected geometric corruption while holding semantics fixed, which is a strong sanity check that the metric measures geometric failure rather than appearance/content shift.

Thorough robustness analyses: correlation of SGC with camera-motion magnitude on real data (showing weak/moderate correlation, i.e., motion-invariance), motion-stratified violin plots, MOS-quality sensitivity analysis, and a 10-fold cross-validation of the PCA aggregation weights showing stability and high rank correlation.

Good ablations isolating the contribution of MOS and the depth-based (vs. grid-based, vs. depth+spatial) sub-region partitioning strategy, plus a construct-validity analysis mapping individual sub-metrics to specific, targeted perturbation types.

Broad coverage of generative paradigms (T2V/I2V/V2V, 10 models) and real-world anchors (nuScenes, RT-1, OpenVid), with qualitative failure-mode diagnostics (warping, incoherent motion, object impermanence, perspective failure) that are convincing and illustrative.
weaknesses: No human study or correlation with human perceptual judgments of geometric (in)consistency is provided; for a proposed evaluation metric intended to guide research and comparisons, this is an important form of validation that is missing (synthetic perturbation monotonicity is a partial but insufficient substitute, since it doesn't establish that SGC differences correspond to perceptually/functionally meaningful degrees of inconsistency).

SGC is built on a stack of off-the-shelf estimators (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA tracking, SegAnyMo) applied to potentially out-of-distribution generated video content; the paper does not analyze how failures/artifacts of these upstream models (e.g., depth or tracking errors on distorted generated frames) might themselves inflate or bias the SGC score, which is a confound for a diagnostic metric whose reliability depends critically on these components.

The final SGC score depends on dataset-level Z-score/min-max normalization and PCA weights computed over a calibration set, meaning individual video scores are not portable/absolute — comparing SGC values across different evaluation pools or after adding/removing models could shift results, undermining standalone interpretability and reproducibility of reported numbers by third parties using different comparison sets.

No code or artifact release is evident (the 'Code:' field is empty), which limits reproducibility given the many implementation-specific choices (clustering hyperparameters, thresholds, PnP-RANSAC settings) enumerated in the appendix.

The MOS-dependency sensitivity analysis reveals non-trivial failure modes (e.g., under-segmentation paradoxically lowering SGC error on some datasets), suggesting the metric's reliability is scene- and segmentation-quality-dependent in ways that could mislead users comparing models with different foreground dynamics.

Baseline comparisons, while reasonably documented, involve several bespoke adaptations (e.g., masked MEt3R via post-hoc score-map masking, custom PCA-based VBench aggregation) that could be seen as tuned specifically to favor SGC's evaluation setup rather than using the baselines' native, established protocols.

strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates a real gap in video-generation evaluation: existing metrics either ignore geometric distortion (FVD, CLIPScore) or penalize valid foreground motion (VBench, NVS metrics), and the paper's framing of 'content-over-motion' vs 'fragility-to-motion' bias is a useful conceptual contribution.

The core idea -- that static background points must obey a single rigid camera transformation, and that divergence among locally estimated poses signals geometric inconsistency -- is physically well-motivated and intuitive.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation effort: controlled synthetic perturbation experiments (warping, perspective squeeze, depth warp) show monotonic score response; ablations examine MOS, depth clustering vs. grid partitioning, and correlation structure among the five atomic sub-metrics; a 10-fold cross-validation of the PCA weights is provided in the appendix.

The benchmark spans a reasonably broad set of 10 generative models (T2V/I2V/V2V) plus three real-video anchors, and qualitative failure-mode visualizations (Figs. 4, 9, 10) help ground the quantitative claims.
The paper attempts to disentangle camera-motion magnitude from genuine geometric instability (ECD analysis), which is a meaningful robustness check that many prior consistency metrics lack.
weaknesses: No human study or correlation with human judgments of geometric consistency is presented anywhere in the paper. For a metric whose entire purpose is to serve as a proxy for perceptible geometric failures, the absence of any human-agreement analysis (e.g., correlation with human ratings of the failure types shown in Fig. 1) is a fundamental gap; all validation is self-referential (synthetic perturbations designed by the authors, or comparisons against other automatic metrics that the paper itself argues are flawed).

The method is essentially an assembly of existing off-the-shelf components (VGGT for pose, Video Depth Anything for depth, SegAnyMo for motion segmentation, DELTA for tracking, PnP-RANSAC, k-means depth clustering, PCA aggregation) with limited technical novelty beyond the combination and weighting scheme; no new model or algorithmic mechanism is proposed.

Circularity/reliability concern: the metric relies on VGGT to estimate a 'global' camera pose that other local poses are compared against, yet VGGT was trained on natural (largely geometrically-consistent) videos. It is unclear how reliable VGGT's global pose and Video Depth Anything's depth estimates remain when applied to videos that are themselves severely geometrically distorted (the very failure cases SGC targets), and this potential failure mode of the upstream estimators is not analyzed.

PCA weights used for the final SGC score appear to be learned on the same 1,196-video dataset (or a heavily overlapping calibration set) that is then used for the main benchmarking results in Table 1, which risks a lack of independence between calibration and evaluation; the paper does not report evaluation on a truly held-out set with weights fixed a priori.

The generative models evaluated (Zeroscope, Modelscope, Latte, Hotshot, early OpenSora, Seine, LaVie) are largely older/weaker open-source models rather than current state-of-the-art systems (e.g., Sora-class, Kling, Veo, Wan, Hunyuan-family models), which limits the practical relevance of the reported findings to today's frontier generative video models.

The 1D depth-clustering strategy for defining 'coherent sub-regions' is fairly coarse (simple k-means on scalar depth values) and the ablation shows it can arbitrarily merge unrelated co-planar but spatially disjoint regions; the justification for why this improves PnP conditioning is somewhat post-hoc and not theoretically grounded.

Computational cost and practicality of the full pipeline (VGGT + video depth + dense tracking + motion segmentation + PnP-RANSAC per subregion, per frame pair) are not discussed, which matters for a metric intended to be a general benchmarking tool.

Writing frequently uses strong absolute language ('strictly isolates', 'rigorously', 'proves') that overstates the strength of evidence relative to what is empirically shown, particularly given the lack of human-perception grounding.
Code repository link is left blank ('Code:'), raising reproducibility concerns at submission time.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper cleanly articulates the 'content-over-motion' bias of fidelity metrics (FVD) versus the 'fragility-to-motion' bias of consistency metrics (VBench, MEt3R, NVS metrics), and proposes a metric that explicitly targets the underserved niche of background geometric rigidity amid valid foreground dynamics.

The core design is physically grounded and interpretable: enforcing that static-background sub-regions must agree on a single camera transformation is a sound geometric principle, and the decomposition into local inter-segment consistency, global pose consistency, and depth consistency gives the metric interpretable, diagnosable sub-components (nicely demonstrated in the qualitative failure-mode analysis in Fig. 10).

Extensive validation effort beyond a single benchmark table: controlled synthetic perturbation experiments demonstrate monotonicity and sensitivity to specific corruption types; correlation analysis with estimated camera dynamics (ECD) supports robustness to motion magnitude; ablations isolate the contribution of MOS and depth-based clustering; and a 10-fold cross-validation of the PCA weighting scheme supports that the metric's aggregation is not overfit to the specific calibration set.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental scope, spanning 10 generative models across T2V/I2V/V2V paradigms and 3 real-world anchor datasets (nuScenes, RT-1, OpenVid), with a large curated benchmark (1,296 videos) and detailed appendix materials (hyperparameters, dataset statistics, per-fold PCA loadings) that aid reproducibility.

The paper convincingly demonstrates cases where SGC diverges from FVD/VBench-BC rankings (e.g., Latte, Modelscope scoring well on FVD/BC but poorly on SGC), which is a meaningful practical contribution showing SGC captures failures other metrics miss.
weaknesses: No human perceptual study is included to validate that SGC scores correlate with human judgments of geometric implausibility; the qualitative figures are illustrative but not a substitute for a systematic human-alignment analysis, which is typically important evidence for a proposed evaluation metric.

The metric is built entirely atop a pipeline of off-the-shelf, learned estimators (VGGT for global pose, Video Depth Anything for depth, SegAnyMo for motion segmentation, DELTA for tracking); errors or domain-shift failures of these models on out-of-distribution generated video content could corrupt SGC scores, and only MOS-quality sensitivity is analyzed in the appendix—no equivalent stress-test is provided for depth or tracking estimator failures, which seems equally important given the pipeline's reliance on them.

There is a potential circularity/confound risk: since the geometry estimators (VGGT, depth) are trained mostly on real-world data, apparent 'geometric inconsistency' scores on generated videos could partly reflect estimator failure on OOD generated content rather than true underlying geometric implausibility in the video itself; this is not explicitly disentangled.

The synthetic perturbation validation, while useful for demonstrating monotonicity, is somewhat expected/tautological since perturbations are injected directly into the same signals (tracks, depth, poses) that the corresponding sub-metrics measure; a more compelling test would perturb only the rendered RGB and infer downstream effects through the full estimation pipeline.

The PCA-based weighting is dataset (calibration-set) dependent; although cross-validation shows reasonable stability, the composition and diversity of the calibration set could still shift relative importance of components for future or unseen generator classes, and this dependency is not deeply examined by varying which generative models are included in calibration.

No discussion of computational cost or scalability, which is relevant given the many-stage pipeline (depth estimation, dense tracking, motion segmentation, multiple PnP solves per sub-region per frame pair) and could limit the metric's practical adoption if very expensive relative to FVD/VBench.
No code link is provided (placeholder only), raising some reproducibility concerns despite detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation.

strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates a real gap in video generation evaluation: existing fidelity metrics (FVD) ignore geometry while consistency metrics (VBench-BC, MEt3R) are confounded by valid foreground motion.

The proposed SGC pipeline is physically well-grounded (rigid background under a single camera transform) and decomposes cleanly into interpretable sub-metrics (local/global rotational and translational variance, depth consistency), which aids diagnostic interpretability.

Extensive empirical validation effort: benchmarking across 10 generative models and 3 real-world datasets, synthetic perturbation studies showing monotonic sensitivity to geometric corruption, motion-stratified analysis disentangling camera motion from structural failure, and a blinded human study showing high correlation (Spearman 0.945) with perceived 3D stability.

Thorough ablations of design choices (MOS necessity, depth-based vs. grid-based clustering, PCA weighting stability via 10-fold cross-validation, and robustness to swapping the underlying geometry estimator, e.g., VGGT vs. Any4D/Page4D) that support the robustness of the metric beyond a single backbone.

Qualitative failure-mode analysis (Fig. 9-10) convincingly ties specific numeric components to identifiable visual artifacts (warping, perspective failure, object impermanence, catastrophic collapse), strengthening the case that the metric is diagnostic rather than just a black-box score.
weaknesses: SGC's normalization and PCA-derived aggregation weights are learned on the same evaluation/calibration dataset used for benchmarking, raising a mild circularity concern about how much the reported rankings depend on this in-domain calibration versus generalizing to unseen distributions of generative artifacts.

The pipeline is a composition of several off-the-shelf, imperfect components (SegAnyMo for motion segmentation, VGGT for global pose, Video Depth Anything for depth, DELTA for tracking); while robustness checks (backbone swap, MOS perturbation) are provided, cumulative/compounding error across this multi-stage pipeline on already artifact-heavy generative video is not fully characterized, and the paper acknowledges lack of absolute error calibration.

No code or public benchmark release is confirmed in the submission (the code link placeholder is empty), which limits reproducibility given the pipeline's many hyperparameters (kseg, PnP thresholds, clustering) and reliance on specific external model versions.

The human study, while a valuable addition, is relatively modest in scale (150 pairs, 7 annotators, aggregated at only 11 entities), which limits the statistical power of the correlation claims relative to other metrics.

By design, SGC explicitly excludes evaluating dynamic/foreground object consistency, meaning it addresses only part of the '3D spatial geometric consistency' problem space suggested by the title; this scope limitation is acknowledged but somewhat undersells the generality implied by the framing.

Several baseline adaptations (e.g., MEt3R(+MOS) masking, VBench PCA-weighted composite) are custom reimplementations by the authors rather than the original protocols, which could subtly favor SGC in comparisons despite the stated intent of fairness.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underserved gap: existing metrics are either insensitive to geometric distortions (FVD, CLIPScore) or fragile to valid foreground motion (MEt3R, VBench-BC), and the paper's framing of 'content-over-motion' vs. 'fragility-to-motion' bias is a clear and useful articulation of the problem.

The core physical principle (static background points must obey a single rigid camera transformation) is sound and interpretable, and the pipeline (MOS masking, depth-based sub-region clustering, per-region PnP pose estimation, divergence aggregation) is a sensible instantiation of this principle.

Extensive empirical validation effort: a 1296-video benchmark spanning T2V/I2V/V2V generative models and real-world anchors, synthetic perturbation studies demonstrating monotonic sensitivity to controlled geometric degradations, cross-estimator robustness checks (VGGT vs. Any4D vs. Page4D, rank correlation >=0.86), a 10-fold cross-validation of PCA weight stability, and a human-alignment study.

Useful ablations isolating the contribution of MOS and the depth-clustering partitioning strategy, and a construct-validity analysis mapping individual component metrics to specific, targeted perturbations (warping -> global rotation variance, depth warp -> depth error, squeeze -> local rotation variance).

Qualitative failure-mode analysis (Fig. 4, 9, 10) is informative and helps interpret what the metric is actually capturing, showing clear cases where SGC diverges meaningfully from FVD/VBench-BC rankings.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely composes existing off-the-shelf components (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, SegAnyMo, DELTA, k-means depth clustering, PnP-RANSAC) rather than introducing new estimation techniques; the contribution is primarily an aggregation/evaluation protocol, which should be judged as such, but this also means much of the reported 'robustness' is inherited from (and bounded by) third-party estimators not designed for artifact-heavy generative video.

Potential circularity in the PCA-based weighting scheme: weights are learned from the same calibration dataset used for the main benchmark comparisons (Table 1) and are also applied to compute the VBench 'weighted' baseline for 'calibration parity,' which risks favoring SGC's own design choices when compared against re-weighted baselines; the 10-fold CV addresses stability but not this deeper circularity concern.

The human study (App. E) is fairly limited: only 150 pairs and 7 annotators, and correlations are computed at the coarse entity level (10 models + 1 merged real group = 11 data points), which is a very small sample for Spearman/Kendall correlation and may not robustly support the claimed superiority over MEt3R/VBench-BC.

Heavy reliance on estimators trained predominantly on real, static-world data to evaluate artifact-laden generative videos raises unresolved domain-shift concerns (acknowledged in Limitations), and while cross-estimator rank correlation is reported, absolute score calibration/estimator-noise disentanglement is explicitly left unaddressed, weakening confidence in absolute SGC values (only relative rankings are validated).

Computational cost and hyperparameter sensitivity are not analyzed: the pipeline chains multiple heavy foundation models (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, SegAnyMo, DELTA) per video, and key hyperparameters (e.g., kseg=10 depth clusters, PnP thresholds) are fixed without a sensitivity study, raising reproducibility and practicality concerns.

Apparent inconsistency/typo in Table 1 (e.g., OpenSora-i's FVD value 751.2137 appears bolded despite not being the best/second-best among generative methods, since Lavie's 679.8203 is lower), suggesting insufficient care in results presentation that undermines confidence in the reported numbers.
No code repository is actually provided (the 'Code:' field on the title page is empty), which limits reproducibility for a metric intended to be adopted as a community evaluation tool.

The claim that SGC is 'inherently robust to natural camera motion' rests on correlation analysis over only three real-world datasets (RT-1, nuScenes, OpenVid), which is a narrow basis for such a general robustness claim, especially given the weak/moderate and inconsistent correlations reported (r=0.17 to 0.52).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly identifies a real gap between fidelity-centric metrics (FVD) that are insensitive to geometric distortion and consistency-focused metrics (VBench-BC, MEt3R, TSED) that are confounded by valid foreground motion, supporting the need for a background-isolated geometric consistency metric.

The core design is physically grounded and interpretable: enforcing that all static-background points obey a single rigid camera transformation, decomposed into local inter-segment consistency, global pose consistency, and depth consistency, gives a diagnostic (not just scalar) evaluation.

Extensive and multi-pronged empirical validation: a 1296-video benchmark spanning T2V/I2V/V2V models and real-world anchors (nuScenes, RT-1, OpenVid); comparison against 7 baselines; controlled synthetic perturbation experiments demonstrating monotonic sensitivity to geometric degradation while holding semantics fixed; motion-stratified analysis showing weak correlation with camera dynamics (ECD) on real data; a human study showing SGC has the highest correlation with human judgments of background stability (rho=0.945) among all tested metrics; and cross-estimator robustness checks (VGGT vs Any4D vs Page4D) showing rank stability (rho>=0.86).

Thorough ablations examining design choices (MOS necessity, depth-based vs. grid-based vs. spatial+depth clustering, PCA weighting via 10-fold cross-validation, sensitivity to segmentation mask quality), which substantiate that each architectural decision is empirically justified rather than arbitrary.

Practical utility as a diagnostic tool: qualitative case studies (Figs. 9-10) tie specific component metrics to specific named failure modes (warping, perspective violation, object impermanence, catastrophic collapse), which is useful for guiding future generative model development.
weaknesses: The full pipeline is a complex composite of multiple off-the-shelf components (VGGT, Video Depth Anything, DELTA tracking, SegAnyMo, depth k-means clustering, PnP-RANSAC, PCA aggregation), each with its own hyperparameters and failure modes; while robustness to estimator substitution is tested, the overall system remains a heavy, multi-stage pipeline whose end-to-end reliability under compounding errors (e.g., simultaneously poor tracking, poor depth, and poor segmentation) is not stress-tested.

No code repository link is provided (the "Code:" field in the header is empty), which raises reproducibility concerns for a metric-based contribution intended for community-wide adoption as a diagnostic benchmark.

The PCA-derived weighting scheme depends on a calibration dataset; although 10-fold cross-validation shows stability on the paper's own dataset, it is unclear how these weights transfer to substantially different video domains/resolutions/frame rates not represented in the 1296-video benchmark, and no external held-out domain test is shown.

The human study, while a valuable addition, aggregates judgments at only an 11-entity level (10 models + 1 real group) for computing Spearman/Kendall correlations, which is a small number of points for correlation estimation and could be sensitive to the particular grouping/binning choice.

The metric is explicitly restricted to static-background rigidity and does not evaluate the internal 3D consistency of dynamic foreground objects (acknowledged as a limitation), which somewhat limits the scope of "3D spatial geometric consistency" the title promises, since foreground geometric plausibility (e.g., limb proportions, object shape stability under motion) is left unaddressed.

Some baseline adaptations (e.g., the custom late-masking MEt3R(+MOS) variant, VBench PCA-based reweighting) are the authors' own reimplementations rather than the original established protocols, which could raise fairness/comparability questions even though the intent (unified evaluation protocol) is reasonable.
